title: First Aid Basics for Regular People

speaker.persona: Volunteer EMT of nine years who teaches free library workshops; warm, calm, a little scattered, full of family and ambulance-shift stories

outlineText:
Welcome and why I teach this
The first few moments
  Check that the scene is safe
  Call emergency services [cues: 911, dispatcher]
Hands-on skills
  CPR basics [cues: chest compressions, AED]
  Choking
  Severe bleeding
  Burns
  Recovery position
Building your own kit
Wrap-up and getting certified

segments.say: Hi everybody, thanks for coming out tonight. I'm Dana, I've been a volunteer EMT for about nine years, and I teach these little sessions whenever somebody lets me.
And honestly, the reason is my dad. He collapsed at my brother's ball game when I was nineteen and I just froze, and a school bus driver stepped in and kept him going till the ambulance came.
He's fine now, by the way, seventy-eight and still yells at umpires, they banned him from the bleachers once, long story, involves a lawn chair.
And that bus driver's gonna come up again when we get to the pushing-on-the-chest part.
Okay. So. Um, let's, let's get into it.
So first, the minute or two before you even touch anybody matters a ton. Everybody wants to rush in, I get it, but there's an order to it.
Step one, stop and look around. Traffic, smoke, a downed power line, broken glass, an unhappy dog? If you get hurt too, now there's two people down and nobody helping.
Take a breath, put gloves on if you have them, and only walk in when it's actually okay. That's not selfish, that's smart.
I'll show you my bag at the end, there's like four pairs of gloves in there, I'm a little paranoid.
Um, hang on, I had a slide for this, oh, no I didn't, sorry, it's just me and the dummy tonight.
Then you get help headed your way. Don't yell somebody call nine one one into a crowd, everybody figures someone else did. Point at one person. You, green hoodie, make the call.
And whoever's on the phone, say where you are first, so if the call drops they still know where to send the truck. And stay on till they say you can hang up.
Alright, where to next... right.
So now the part where you actually do stuff with your own two hands. The big scary situations, the ones where minutes really count.
The big one, when somebody's heart just quits on them. They go down, don't respond when you tap them and shout, and aren't breathing normally, and those weird gasping, snoring breaths do not count.
Heel of your hand in the center of the chest, other hand on top, push hard and fast, about two inches down, a hundred to a hundred and twenty a minute, and let it come all the way back up.
That's all the bus driver did for my dad, like I said at the start, she'd never had a class, and she kept it up for eleven minutes.
And if anybody spots one of those defibrillator boxes on the wall, send someone for it and switch it on. It talks you through it, it's really hard to mess up.
Totally unrelated, but whoever brought the lemon bars, thank you, I've had three, and I'm taking the rest home unless someone stops me.
Now a different kind of scary, because this person's still awake. Somebody's at dinner, grabs at their throat, can't talk, can't cough, going a little blue. A bite of steak went down and it's stuck.
If they're coughing hard, cheer them on. If they can't, get behind them, five firm smacks between the shoulder blades, then five quick upward squeezes above the belly button, and keep switching.
Um, where was I, sorry, I wrote this on an index card and now I can't read my own handwriting.

If it's a tiny baby with something stuck, it's different. Face down along your forearm, head low, five firm back slaps with the heel of your hand, then flip them and press the breastbone with two fingers. No belly squeezes on an infant.
And if the person with the stuck bite goes limp on you, ease them to the floor and, yep, you're back to that hard fast pushing from before.
Okay, blood. If somebody's got a deep cut and it's really pouring or spurting, grab any clean cloth, a T-shirt, a dish towel, and press down hard, lean your weight into it.
Don't keep lifting it to peek, if it soaks through, pile more on. On an arm or leg, if that's not enough, a tourniquet goes on a few inches above the wound, tight till it stops, and note the time.
So then, once someone's through the worst of it, and they're breathing but out of it, not waking up, you don't want to leave them flat on their back.
Roll them onto their side, top knee bent so they don't tip forward, hand under their cheek, head tipped back a little so the airway stays open, and if they throw up it runs out of their mouth.
Oh shoot, wait, I skipped one. The kitchen one! Hot pans, boiling water, curling irons, I've got a scar from a sheet pan, how did I skip that.
Get it under cool running water, not ice, not butter, whatever grandma said, and keep it there like twenty minutes, which feels like forever. Pull off rings before it swells.
Then cover it loosely with something clean that won't stick, plastic kitchen wrap works great, and don't pop the blisters. If it's big, or on the face or hands, or from chemicals, get it seen.
Kind of like with the cut, you're putting something clean over it, but here you lay it on gently, no pressing, the total opposite of the bleeding.
Okay, back on track. The bag! You want the stuff for all this somewhere you can grab it fast, one in the house, one in the car.
In mine: gloves, bandages in all sizes, gauze pads, a roll of wrap, tape, blunt-tip shears, a store-bought tourniquet, a little face shield for rescue breaths, and a foil blanket.
And go through it every six months. Stuff expires, gloves get brittle, and the little bandages all got used on splinters. I do mine when the clocks change.
Okay, um, so, last thing.
Tonight is a taste, not a certification. Please take a proper class, the Red Cross or your fire department runs them all the time, and it sticks way better once your hands have done it.
And people always ask about getting sued. Most places have Good Samaritan laws that protect you when you help in good faith. So doing something beats standing there frozen, like I did.
